title: Modifié Denver critères pour Blunt Cerebrovascular lésion (BCVI)
formula:
The Modified Denver Criteria forBCVIare met when a patient presents with one or more of the specified signs of a high-energy transfer mechanism:

| Modified Denver Criteria for BCVI |
| --- |
| Le Fort II or III fracture |
| Basilar skull fracture with carotid canal involvement |
| Diffuse axonal injury with [GCS](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs\) <6 |
| Cervical spine fracture patterns |
| Near-hanging with anoxic brain injury |

how_to_use.why:
- BCVI is often clinically occult; without structured screening, up to 30%–35% of injuries are missed, placing patients at high risk for ischemic stroke (up to 46% if untreated) and stroke-related mortality (~32%).
- This tool offers a standardized approach to identify patients at increased risk after blunt trauma and helps guide when CTA of the neck should be considered.
how_to_use.when: À appliquer aux patients présentant un traumatisme contondant afin d’identifier ceux qui pourraient bénéficier d’une angiographie par tomodensitométrie (CTA) du cou pour rechercher une lésion cérébrovasculaire contondante (BCVI).
how_to_use.pearls:
- Any single criterion (sign/symptom or risk factor) is sufficient to warrant consideration of CTA of the neck.
- BCVI can present with delayed neurologic deficits, so do not rely on symptoms alone; mechanism and injury patterns also matter.
- Even expanded criteria may miss BCVI, leading some trauma centers to adopt more liberal CTA strategies in selected blunt trauma populations.
- Use this tool to guide, not replace, clinical judgment; a thorough trauma evaluation and neurologic assessment remain essential.

next_steps.advice:
- Cet outil aide à identifier les patients susceptibles de bénéficier d'un dépistage par CTA du cou pour une BCVI après un traumatisme fermé.
- Interpréter les résultats dans le contexte du tableau clinique global, incluant le mécanisme lésionnel, les lésions associées et l'évolution de l'examen neurologique.
next_steps.critical_actions: Aggressive BCVI screening and early anticoagulant therapy are associated with a significant reduction in ischemic neurologic events.
next_steps.management:
- **Si l'un quelconque des critères est rempli,** envisager une évaluation plus approfondie à la recherche d'une BCVI possible par CTA du cou.
- **Si aucun critère n'est présent,** la sensibilité du dépistage n'est pas absolue ; une préoccupation persistante fondée sur le mécanisme, des symptômes évolutifs ou le jugement clinique peut encore justifier une imagerie.

evidence:
**Foundational Evidence: Original Denver Data**

In a prospective 7-year study at a level I trauma center,[Cothren et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15136355/)evaluated 13,280 patients with blunt trauma using a predefined screening protocol based on high-energy mechanism, associated injury patterns (e.g., LeFort II/III fractures, basilar skull fracture with carotid canal involvement, cervical spine fracture), and neurologic symptoms to identify patients at risk for blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI). Using this structured approach, 643 patients underwent angiography and 114 were found to have blunt carotid artery injury (overall incidence 0.86% of all trauma admissions), demonstrating that these injuries are substantially more common than previously believed. Historically, as referenced in prior literature cited in this study, more than 90% of BCVI cases were diagnosed only after neurologic symptoms occurred, meaning the majority were missed when clinicians relied on symptoms alone.

The consequences of missed or untreated BCVI were substantial: 46% of patients who did not receive anticoagulation developed an ischemic neurologic event, compared to 0% of the 73 asymptomatic patients who were promptly anticoagulated. This finding was consistent across heparin, LMWH, and antiplatelet therapy. Stroke-related mortality in the cohort reached 32% (6 of 19 patients), and the average onset of neurologic symptoms occurred within a “latent window” of approximately 50–77 hours post-injury, reinforcing that early identification before symptom onset is time-critical for preventing stroke. The authors conclude that BCVI is often occult, clinically silent, and only uncovered through intentional screening, and that early diagnosis with prompt anticoagulation significantly reduces morbidity and mortality. This work provides foundational rationale for clinical decision tools like the Modified Denver Criteria to guide which trauma patients require vascular imaging.

**Why Screening Criteria Became Necessary**

Building on this work,[Biffl et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10670864/)analyzed patients undergoing angiography for suspected BCVI and identified independent predictors of carotid and vertebral artery injury, including [Glasgow Coma Scale](nabda:calc.glasgow-coma-scale-score-gcs) ≤6, petrous bone fracture, diffuse axonal brain injury, and LeFort II/III fractures. Among patients with a high-risk mechanism and at least one of these predictors, the risk of carotid injury was approximately 41%, and about 39% of patients with cervical spine fracture had a vertebral artery injury. These findings supported the development and refinement of the Denver, Modified Denver, and Expanded Denver Criteria, formalizing mechanism- and injury-based screening to select trauma patients for cerebrovascular imaging rather than relying on neurologic symptoms alone.

**Modern Validating Evidence**

More recent multicenter and population-level studies confirm that BCVI is both more common and more clinically significant than earlier estimates suggested, with reported incidence ranging from about 1% of all patients with blunt trauma up to 2.7% in centers using liberal or universal CTA-based screening protocols. Left untreated, BCVI is associated with reported stroke rates of 9%–11% and mortality of 16%–27%, underscoring the high stakes of missed injury.

Importantly, contemporary work also suggests that reliance on Denver-based criteria alone can miss a meaningful subset of patients. In one[multi-institution cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36841698/), 30%–35% of BCVIs would have been missed by the Denver and Expanded Denver Criteria compared with a liberalized CTA approach, and[another series](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36101794/)found that 16% of patients with BCVI had none of the Expanded Denver risk factors and would not have been screened under guideline-only strategies. A[universal screening protocol](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32520898/)found that 23% of patients with grade ≥3 BCVI (clinically significant injuries) lacked any established screening criteria.

Despite these limitations, Denver-based predictors remain the most validated framework for risk stratification, and treatment after BCVI diagnosis is impactful. In one[universal-screening cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32520898/), 83% of patients received antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy, with only 4% bleeding complications, 3% progression, and 8% stroke, supporting the clinical value of early BCVI detection and justifying the use of structured tools such as the Modified Denver Criteria to guide imaging decisions.
